title: Joshua's Filthy Garments and the Branch
summary: In the fourth vision Zechariah sees Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of the LORD in filthy clothes, with Satan at his right hand to accuse him. The LORD rebukes the accuser, Joshua's filthy garments are removed and replaced with clean robes and a turban, and he is charged to walk in God's ways. God then promises to bring his servant the Branch and to remove the guilt of the land in a single day.
story: The first three visions spoke of God's return to Jerusalem, the fall of Judah's enemies, and a city overflowing with people. But one question remained. Could a people whose sins had brought the exile stand before a holy God again? Could a priesthood that had failed be trusted to serve in a new temple? This vision answers by showing the high priest, the representative of the whole people, accused and defiled, and then cleansed by God's own act. It stands alongside the next vision (chapter 4), which concerns Zerubbabel, the other leader of the community, and together they place the priest and the prince at the center of the book's first half.
historical:
Joshua son of Jehozadak (called Jeshua in Ezra and Nehemiah) was the first high priest after the exile. His father Jehozadak had been taken into exile by the Babylonians (1 Chronicles 6:15), and his grandfather Seraiah, the chief priest when Jerusalem fell, was executed by Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah (2 Kings 25:18-21). Joshua had returned with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:2; 3:2) and led in rebuilding the altar. Around 519 BC, as the temple rose, the question of his fitness to serve would have been pressing: a priest who had grown up in an unclean foreign land, from a priestly line the earlier prophets had condemned (Jeremiah 23:11; Ezekiel 22:26), was about to minister in God's house.

The promise of the Branch picks up Jeremiah's earlier prophecy that God would raise up for David a righteous Branch (Jeremiah 23:5; 33:15). In Zechariah's day the royal line of David was represented by Zerubbabel, who ruled as a Persian governor rather than a king.
cultural:
The scene is a heavenly law court. In the ancient Near East an accuser stood at the right hand of the accused, as Psalm 109:6 also pictures. The Hebrew has the satan, with the article, meaning the accuser or adversary, a figure who appears in a similar role in the heavenly court in Job 1 and 2. Whether the word is used here as a personal name or as a title is debated, but the role is clear: he stands to bring charges.

The clothing matters because of the priestly law. The high priest wore specially made garments for glory and beauty (Exodus 28:2), and a turban bearing a gold plate inscribed Holy to the LORD (Exodus 28:36-38). Priests had to be ritually clean to serve, and the word for Joshua's clothes in verses 3 and 4 is an unusually strong one, connected in Hebrew with excrement. A defiled high priest could not represent the people, and a defiled people could not approach God. Sitting under one's own vine and fig tree (verse 10) was a proverbial picture of peace and security, used of Solomon's reign (1 Kings 4:25) and of the coming age (Micah 4:4).
literary: Unlike the earlier visions, this one begins without a question from the prophet; Zechariah simply sees, and at one point he speaks up himself, asking that a clean turban be put on Joshua's head. The scene moves from accusation (verses 1-2), to cleansing (verses 3-5), to charge (verses 6-7), to promise (verses 8-10), and in doing so it moves from Joshua's person to his companions, to the coming Branch, to the whole land. The image of a firebrand snatched from the fire (verse 2) comes from Amos 4:11 and pictures a stick pulled half-burned from the flames, a survivor of judgment.

outline.t: Joshua accused, and the LORD rebukes Satan
Filthy garments removed, clean robes given
The Branch, the stone, and the guilt removed in one day

doctrines.note: Joshua does nothing to cleanse himself. He stands silent while God answers the accuser, removes his filthy clothes, and dresses him. God says, I have removed your iniquity, and the clean clothing is a gift, not an achievement. This is a vivid picture of grace.

God promises to remove the iniquity of the land in a single day (verse 9). The phrase echoes the Day of Atonement, when the high priest made atonement for the whole people once a year, and points to a decisive cleansing beyond what that yearly day could accomplish.
The Branch is a title for the coming king of David's line, drawn from Jeremiah. Here he is called God's servant and linked with the priesthood: Joshua and his companions are a sign that he is coming.

words.note: Satan, adversary or accuser. The word is used of human opponents (1 Kings 11:14) and of a heavenly accuser (Job 1 and 2). Here it has the article, the adversary, and stands with the related verb in verse 1, standing to accuse him. His role is to charge, and the LORD's role is to rebuke the charge.

Tsemach, sprout or branch, something that springs up from the ground. Jeremiah used it for the righteous Branch God would raise up for David (Jeremiah 23:5). Zechariah makes it a title, my servant, the Branch, and uses it again in 6:12. The image suggests new growth from a stump that seemed dead.

Avon, iniquity or guilt. The word can mean the wrong done, the guilt it brings, or the punishment it deserves. Here God removes it from Joshua personally (verse 4) and promises to remove it from the whole land in one day (verse 9).

Mopheth, a sign or wonder, an event or person that points beyond itself. Joshua and his companions are men of sign: their cleansed priesthood is a pledge that God's greater work, the Branch, is on its way.

christ: Christians have long read this vision as one of the Old Testament's clearest pictures of the gospel, though its link to Christ comes through its promises and patterns rather than a direct prediction of Jesus's life. The Branch, God's servant from David's line, is the Messiah whom the New Testament identifies with Jesus. The removal of iniquity in a single day is fulfilled, in the New Testament's reading, in Christ's once-for-all sacrifice, which Hebrews contrasts with the high priest's repeated yearly offering (Hebrews 9:25-28; 10:10-14). The heavenly courtroom scene, with an accuser silenced and a guilty man clothed in clean garments, anticipates Paul's question, who will bring any charge against God's elect? (Romans 8:33-34), and Revelation's picture of the accuser of our brothers thrown down (Revelation 12:10). The name Joshua is the Hebrew form of the name Jesus, a coincidence that early Christian readers noticed, though the text itself makes nothing of it.

hard.q: What is the stone with seven eyes in verse 9?
hard.a: This is one of the book's puzzles, and interpreters disagree. Some take the stone as a precious stone for the high priest's clothing, perhaps the gold plate on the turban, which was engraved with an inscription (Exodus 28:36); the verb for engrave here is the same one used there. Others take it as a building stone for the temple, perhaps the capstone or foundation stone connected with Zerubbabel in 4:7-10. The seven eyes may be read as facets, as springs (the Hebrew word for eye can also mean spring), or as the eyes of the LORD that range over the whole earth, as in 4:10. Many Christian readers connect the stone with the messianic stone of Psalm 118:22 and Isaiah 28:16, which the New Testament applies to Christ. The context is clear about the point even where the image is obscure: God is preparing something that will lead to the removal of the land's guilt in one day.

questions: Joshua stood silent while the accuser spoke and God answered. What accusations, true or false, do you find hardest to leave in God's hands?
God gave Joshua clean clothes before charging him to walk in his ways. Why does the order matter, grace first and then obedience?
The chapter ends with neighbors inviting each other under vine and fig tree. What does forgiveness have to do with peace between people?
